questions.question: What kinds of old photos do users struggle to retrieve when their memory is incomplete?
questions.key_finding: Users struggle most with candid, non-albumed episodic events (spontaneous meals, roadside cafes, casual outings), utility items with fuzzy visual text (prescriptions, model numbers, handwritten notes), and memories defined by emotional context rather than iconic landmarks.
evidence_quotes: I spent 45 minutes trying to find that picture of the seafood paella we ate at a beach shack during our Valencia trip three years ago. I searched 'paella beach', 'spain seafood', 'beach restaurant', and got either random beach pictures or nothing.

Trying to find an old prescription medicine bottle photo from last winter. When I search 'medicine' or 'prescription', Google Photos gives me dozens of random WhatsApp screenshots, insurance paperwork, and memes.
questions.pm_implication: Retrieval engines are optimized for nouns and geotagged landmarks, but human episodic memory is anchored in personal activities, shared meals, and informal moments.

questions.question: What information do people actually remember about a photo, and what have they forgotten?
questions.key_finding: Users vividly remember relative timeframes ('two summers ago', 'right after moving'), emotional sentiment ('hilarious moment', 'exhausting hike'), companion presence, and distinctive visual fragments ('she wore a bright yellow raincoat'). They almost never remember exact calendar dates, camera file names, or formal venue names.
evidence_quotes: I don't remember the exact restaurant name or the date, so I had to endlessly scroll through August 2023 until my eyes hurt.
I know the photo exists, it was taken right around Thanksgiving at my sister's house, but search brings up zero results for family dinner.
questions.pm_implication: Search UI must allow expressive multi-modal query inputs that match human recall patterns rather than rigid SQL-like filters.

questions.question: Where does retrieval break down across expression, interpretation, evaluation, and recovery?
questions.key_finding: Interpretation (41%) is the primary breakdown where keyword search fails to parse compound clues and Ask Photos misinterprets conversational nuance. Recovery (26%) is the second critical friction where failed searches offer zero refinement options, forcing abandonment to manual scrolling.
evidence_quotes: Asked Gemini to find 'the picture of my dog wearing a yellow raincoat in the snow' and it just gave me random pictures of my cat and summer grass.
I searched every variation of paella, beach, and Spain I could think of. Every retry cleared my search and gave zero results.
questions.pm_implication: Investing solely in better initial search is insufficient; adding contextual refinement chips and conversational disambiguation turns failure into discovery.

questions.question: How do traditional keyword search and Gemini-based AI search compare in these failure modes?
questions.key_finding: Traditional keyword search suffers from extreme literalism (0 results if exact text isn't in metadata/OCR) and lack of relative-time handling. Gemini AI search solves vocabulary matching but introduces hallucination, over-confidence, and conversational dead-ends where follow-up questions fail to narrow results.
evidence_quotes: Ask Photos sounded amazing, but whenever I ask for a specific document or photo, it either hallucinates or gives me a generic error saying it can't find anything.
Keyword search gives zero results if you misspell one word or don't know the exact year.
questions.pm_implication: A hybrid architecture combining Gemini's semantic understanding with deterministic metadata bounding and interactive visual refinement chips yields the highest retrieval success rate.
